assumption:consistency.in_more_depth: Consistency is what makes "the effect of X" mean anything. It is comfortable for a drug at a stated dose and uncomfortable for "obesity", "education" or "democracy", where the intervention is not defined and different ways of changing the variable would have different effects. Target-trial thinking is the discipline here: write down the trial you would run, including who is eligible, when time zero is, and what exactly is assigned. If you cannot write it, the estimand is not yet a question.
assumption:consistency.one_liner: The outcome you observe under the treatment a unit received is the same as the potential outcome under that treatment. In practice: the treatment has to be a thing someone could actually do.
assumption:consistency.plain_language: The outcome you observe under the treatment a unit received is the same as the potential outcome under that treatment. In practice: the treatment has to be a thing someone could actually do.

assumption:continuity.in_more_depth: The cutoff has to be doing one job. If the same threshold also triggers a different programme, a tax band or an administrative category, the jump you measure is the combined effect of all of them, and nothing separates them. Continuity is why the estimate is local: it is identified at the cutoff and the extrapolation away from it is a modelling choice, not a finding.

assumption:convex_hull.in_more_depth: Classic synthetic control restricts weights to be non-negative and to sum to one, which forbids extrapolation on purpose. The price is that if the treated unit is more extreme than every donor -- richer, larger, more urban -- no combination can reach it, and the synthetic unit is biased towards the middle of the pool. That bias then shows up as a permanent gap that looks like an effect. Augmented synthetic control corrects for that bias explicitly, and reports the size of the correction so you can see how much work it is doing.
assumption:convex_hull.one_liner: The treated unit's characteristics can be written as a weighted average of the donors', with weights that do not go negative.
assumption:convex_hull.plain_language: The treated unit's characteristics can be written as a weighted average of the donors', with weights that do not go negative.

assumption:donor_fit.in_more_depth: A synthetic control that cannot track the treated unit before the intervention has no claim to track it after. Pre-period fit is the closest thing to a testable condition this design has, and it is a necessary condition rather than a sufficient one: a good pre-fit can still be a coincidence, especially with a short pre-period and many donors. Report the pre-period root-mean-square prediction error, and compare it with the same quantity for placebo units. A treated unit whose post/pre error ratio is unremarkable among the placebos has not shown an effect.
assumption:donor_fit.one_liner: The weighted combination of untreated units reproduces the treated unit's pre-period path closely enough to stand in for it afterwards.

assumption:exchangeability.in_more_depth: This is the assumption the whole selection-on-observables design rests on, and no diagnostic in this product can test it. Balance plots show that the variables you measured are now comparable; they say nothing about the ones you did not measure. A perfectly flat Love plot is consistent with total confounding by something you never recorded. What you can do instead: argue from how treatment was actually assigned, draw the graph and see whether your adjustment set closes the back doors, and then ask the sensitivity question -- how strong would an unmeasured confounder have to be, compared with the ones you did measure, before the conclusion changes?
assumption:exchangeability.one_liner: Treated and untreated units are comparable once you condition on the confounders you measured. Everything that pushed people towards treatment and also moves the outcome is in your adjustment set.
assumption:exchangeability.plain_language: Treated and untreated units are comparable once you condition on the confounders you measured. Everything that pushed people towards treatment and also moves the outcome is in your adjustment set.

assumption:exclusion.in_more_depth: Exclusion cannot be tested. A strong first stage tells you the instrument moves treatment; it tells you nothing about whether it also moves the outcome another way. Overidentification tests compare instruments against each other and are silent when all of them are invalid in the same direction. What you can do: argue from how the instrument was generated, and look for placebo outcomes the instrument should not affect. Finding an effect there is evidence against exclusion; finding none is weak comfort.
assumption:exclusion.one_liner: The instrument affects the outcome only through the treatment. On the board, that is the arrow you did not draw.
assumption:exclusion.plain_language: The instrument affects the outcome only through the treatment. On the board, that is the arrow you did not draw.

assumption:model_form.in_more_depth: This is an assumption, not an estimate, and it is doing more work than any coefficient in the model. A linear pre-trend extrapolated over several years is a strong claim. Seasonality, mean reversion after an unusual year, and slow-moving demographics all bend the counterfactual. Autocorrelated residuals are the standard failure: ordinary standard errors then understate uncertainty badly, sometimes by a factor of two or three.

assumption:monotonicity.in_more_depth: Without monotonicity, the instrumental-variables estimate is a mixture of compliers' and defiers' effects with weights that can be negative, and it need not lie between the effects of any real group. It is not testable, though the implied complier share and the proportions of each response type give a sanity check: a negative implied share is evidence something is wrong.

assumption:no_anticipation.in_more_depth: Announcement usually precedes implementation, and people respond to announcements. If they do, the "before" period is already partly treated, which biases the comparison and can make the pre-trend look wrong even when parallel trends holds. The pre-period coefficients of an event study are where anticipation shows up: a drift starting exactly at the announcement date is the signature. Interrupted-time-series designs let you mark announcement and implementation as two separate dates for this reason.
assumption:no_anticipation.one_liner: Units did not change behaviour before treatment arrived because they knew it was coming.
assumption:no_anticipation.plain_language: Units did not change behaviour before treatment arrived because they knew it was coming.

assumption:no_cointerventions.in_more_depth: An interrupted time series attributes the whole break to the policy. Policy rarely arrives alone: a smoking ban lands with a media campaign, a lockdown with a benefits change, a guideline with a payment reform. Any of those would produce the same picture. A control series that should have been unaffected is the main defence. If the control breaks at the same moment, something broader happened.

assumption:no_manipulation.in_more_depth: Regression discontinuity works because, right at the cutoff, which side you fall on is as good as random. That fails if people can fine-tune their score: applicants who just miss a threshold and resubmit, firms that report just under a reporting limit, students whose marks get nudged over a pass line. The density test is the standard check: if there is a cliff in the number of units just either side of the cutoff, someone was sorting. A smooth density does not prove there was no manipulation, but a jump is strong evidence there was. Covariate balance at the cutoff is the second check: pre-determined characteristics should not jump.
assumption:no_manipulation.one_liner: People could not precisely control which side of the cutoff they landed on.
assumption:no_manipulation.plain_language: People could not precisely control which side of the cutoff they landed on.

assumption:no_time_varying_confounding.in_more_depth: In longitudinal data the same variable is often a confounder for later treatment and a consequence of earlier treatment. Adjusting for it in an ordinary regression both blocks the path you want and opens a collider path; not adjusting for it leaves confounding. This is precisely the problem g-methods were invented for. Lag discipline is the practical form of this assumption: a covariate may adjust a treatment decision only if it was measured before that decision. The board draws arrows that cannot point into the future for this reason.
assumption:no_time_varying_confounding.one_liner: At every period, the things that drive the treatment decision and also affect the outcome are measured -- and measured before that decision.
assumption:no_time_varying_confounding.plain_language: At every period, the things that drive the treatment decision and also affect the outcome are measured -- and measured before that decision.

assumption:parallel_trends.common_mistake: Reading a pre-trend test that fails to reject as confirmation. Low power makes that easy, and a wide pre-period confidence interval is not evidence of parallel paths.

assumption:parallel_trends.in_more_depth: This is the identifying assumption of difference-in-differences, and it is about a counterfactual path nobody observes. The pre-period is the closest thing to evidence: if the groups already moved differently before the policy, the assumption is in trouble. If they moved together, that is consistent with parallel trends and also consistent with them diverging afterwards for reasons unrelated to the policy. Parallel trends is also scale-dependent: trends parallel in levels are generally not parallel in logs. Choosing the scale is part of the assumption, not a presentation detail. When pre-trends are imperfect, honest DiD asks the useful question: how much could trends have drifted before the conclusion breaks?
assumption:parallel_trends.one_liner: Without the policy, treated and comparison groups would have moved the same way. Not that they were at the same level -- that their paths would have been parallel.
assumption:parallel_trends.plain_language: Without the policy, treated and comparison groups would have moved the same way. Not that they were at the same level -- that their paths would have been parallel.
references: Roth (2022), Pretest with caution

assumption:positivity.in_more_depth: Positivity is the assumption you actually can look at. Fit a treatment model, plot the predicted probabilities by arm, and see whether the two distributions overlap. Where treated units sit at probabilities no control unit reaches, the estimate for those units comes from extrapolating the outcome model, not from anything in the data. The effective sample size is the honest denominator: reweighting a comparison group to look like the treated group can leave you with a thousand rows worth a hundred observations. Structural violations (a rule that made some group ineligible) cannot be fixed by any estimator. Random violations (a small sample in a thin region) show up as unstable weights.
assumption:positivity.one_liner: Every kind of unit had some chance of being treated and some chance of not being treated. Where that fails, there is no comparison to make and the model is inventing one.
assumption:positivity.plain_language: Every kind of unit had some chance of being treated and some chance of not being treated. Where that fails, there is no comparison to make and the model is inventing one.

assumption:randomisation.in_more_depth: In a clean experiment this is the assumption that does all the work, and it is the one you get for free. What is not free is what happened afterwards. Attrition that differs by arm, treatment received that differs from treatment assigned, and outcomes measured differently by arm all break the guarantee. A baseline balance table checks that nothing went wrong in the mechanics. It is not a test of randomisation: with enough covariates some will differ by chance, and a failed balance test on a genuinely randomised trial is a false alarm as often as a real signal.

assumption:relevance.in_more_depth: This one is testable, and the test matters more than people expect. assumption:sequential_ignorability.in_more_depth: Mediation asks for two exchangeability assumptions instead of one, and the second is usually much harder: whatever determines how much of the mediator a person gets is rarely unrelated to their outcome. Natural direct and indirect effects need a third, cross-world condition relating potential outcomes under treatment values that no single person can ever experience. No experiment, however large, can test it. That is why interventional (stochastic) effects are the better default in policy and health: they answer a slightly different question that a trial could in principle check.

concept:concept.about.in_more_depth: The object of work here is a causal question, not an equation. You state the question in ordinary language, complete a picture of the research design, look at the diagnostics that design depends on, and then estimate -- usually with several methods at once, because the disagreement between them is part of what you learned. Everything runs locally. Your data does not leave this machine unless you export it, and there is no telemetry. The engines are the R and Python packages the field already publishes with; this application orchestrates them, records what was assumed, and refuses to present an estimate as causal because of the estimator's name. concept:concept.caliper.in_more_depth: Matching pairs each treated unit with the most similar untreated one available -- but "the most similar available" can still be very dissimilar when the comparison pool is thin. A caliper puts a bound on the gap, usually stated as a fraction of the spread of the estimated treatment probability, and refuses the pair when nothing falls inside it. The trade is explicit. A tight caliper gives better-matched pairs and drops more treated units; a loose one keeps everybody and admits worse comparisons. The dropping is not just a loss of precision: the question changes with it, because the answer now describes the treated units that could be matched rather than all of them. That is why the count of unmatched treated units belongs beside the estimate rather than in a footnote.
concept:concept.caliper.one_liner: The largest difference you are willing to tolerate inside a matched pair. Beyond it the treated unit is left unmatched rather than paired with somebody unlike them.
concept:concept.caliper.plain_language: The largest difference you are willing to tolerate inside a matched pair. Beyond it the treated unit is left unmatched rather than paired with somebody unlike them.

concept:concept.cluster_robust_se.common_mistake: Clustering at the wrong level -- on the individual when assignment was by school, or on the year when the policy varied by state. The rule is to cluster at the level treatment was assigned.

concept:concept.cluster_robust_se.in_more_depth: If a whole school was assigned to the programme together, its pupils do not each carry separate evidence about whether the programme works: they share a headteacher, a catchment and a year. An interval computed as though the pupils were independent counts the same information over and over and comes out far too narrow, so an effect looks settled when it is not. The cluster-robust version allows rows within a group to be related in any way at all, and assumes only that different groups are independent of each other. What it needs in return is enough groups. Its accuracy grows with the number of clusters, not the number of rows, and with only a couple of dozen it becomes optimistic again -- which is the point at which a small-sample correction, or reshuffling whole clusters at a time, is the safer route.
concept:concept.cluster_robust_se.one_liner: A way of computing uncertainty that treats each group -- a school, a village, a clinic -- as one group's worth of independent evidence, rather than counting every row inside it separately.
concept:concept.cluster_robust_se.plain_language: A way of computing uncertainty that treats each group -- a school, a village, a clinic -- as one group's worth of independent evidence, rather than counting every row inside it separately.

concept:concept.clustering.in_more_depth: Standard errors that ignore the group structure can be several times too small, which turns a null result into a finding. The rule of thumb is to cluster at the level treatment was assigned at, which is usually coarser than the level the data is stored at. With few clusters -- under about forty -- the usual cluster-robust correction is itself unreliable, and the honest move is a small-sample correction, a t distribution with the number of clusters minus one, or a cluster bootstrap. This product states which one it used on every result.

concept:concept.collider.common_mistake: Treating "adjust for more covariates" as always safer. Colliders and post-treatment variables make it worse.
concept:concept.collider.in_more_depth: Suppose talent and looks both help an actor get hired, and are unrelated in the population. Among people who were hired, the two become negatively related: if someone got in without much talent, they probably had looks. Nothing caused that association except your decision to look only at the hired. The same thing happens whenever you adjust for a variable that treatment and outcome both influence, or condition on a sample selected on such a variable. It is bias you added.

concept:concept.complete_case.in_more_depth: The rows that survive are not a random sample of the rows you started with. If the people doing badly were also the ones more likely to skip the follow-up, the surviving sample is healthier than the population it is meant to describe, and every number computed on it inherits that. The bias can run in either direction, and how large it is cannot be read off the rows that remain. It is not always wrong. If whatever drove the missingness is unrelated to the outcome once you account for the variables you kept, complete cases are unbiased and merely less precise. The honest minimum is to report how many rows went, and whether they went from the treated and untreated groups at the same rate.

concept:concept.confounding.in_more_depth: If healthier people are both more likely to take a drug and more likely to survive, the drug looks effective whether or not it is. Adjusting means comparing treated and untreated units that match on the common cause, so that the remaining difference cannot be explained by it. The hard part is not the arithmetic; it is knowing what the common causes are. Adjustment can only handle the ones you measured, which is why the exchangeability assumption stays untested no matter how good the balance plot looks.

concept:concept.cross_fitting.in_more_depth: Machine-learning models for the treatment and outcome overfit, and if the same rows fit the model and enter the score, the overfitting shows up as bias in the estimate and as a confidence interval that is too narrow. Splitting into folds, fitting on the complement and predicting on the held- out fold removes that route, at the price of a little variance. It is what makes double machine learning honest, and it is why the fold diagnostics are mandatory whenever a learner is used: if the estimate swings wildly across folds, the answer depends on the split.

concept:concept.donor_pool.common_mistake: Treating the pool as given because it arrived with the dataset. Write down why each unit is in it and why the excluded ones are out; that list is part of the design and belongs in the write-up.

concept:concept.donor_pool.in_more_depth: A synthetic control builds its stand-in by blending other units, and it can only blend the ones you put in front of it. Include somewhere that got its own version of the policy and the comparison is contaminated by it. Include somewhere with nothing in common with the treated place and it will simply receive a weight of zero -- harmless, but it makes the pool look larger than it really is. Leave out the one place that would have matched well and the fit suffers for a reason nothing in the output will name. The pool also fixes how strong the placebo evidence can be. The treated unit's gap is judged against the gaps you get by pretending each donor was treated instead, so five donors give five comparisons, and "more extreme than all of them" is a one-in-six statement. No amount of computing makes it a stronger one.
concept:concept.donor_pool.one_liner: The set of untreated places a synthetic comparison is allowed to be built from. Choosing it is a research decision, not a technical one.

concept:concept.effective_sample_size.in_more_depth: Weighting a comparison group to resemble the treated group concentrates the analysis on the few comparison units that actually resemble them. Kish's effective sample size expresses that concentration as a count: a thousand rows with wildly unequal weights can be worth eighty observations. It is the honest denominator. When it collapses, the confidence interval is narrower than the evidence, and the estimate rests on a handful of units whose individual peculiarities now matter.

This product therefore shows a headline number only when exactly one method ran; otherwise the range across defensible methods is the finding, and the generated prose describes the range. You can nominate a preferred estimate for a report. It is stored as a choice and displayed as a choice, not as a conclusion.

concept:concept.honest_splitting.in_more_depth: If the same rows choose the split and estimate the effect inside it, the estimate is biased upwards by construction: the split was chosen because the effect looked large there. Honest trees and honest forests avoid it by separating the two jobs inside every tree. The price is variance -- half the rows for each job -- which is why honest methods need more data than they first appear to. The reward is a heterogeneity estimate you can believe.

concept:concept.multiplicity.in_more_depth: With twenty subgroups and no real heterogeneity, you expect one significant result at the 5% level. The problem is not the arithmetic, it is that the subgroup gets written up as a finding and the other nineteen do not appear. Causal Capybara marks subgroup estimates as a separate group in the results and attaches a multiplicity caution rather than presenting them as a table of independent findings. For discovered rather than pre-specified heterogeneity, the calibration test and the rank-weighted effect are the honest summaries.

concept:concept.negative_control.in_more_depth: If a vaccine appears to prevent injuries as well as influenza, the apparent influenza effect is at least partly healthy-user bias. That is more useful than any test of balance, because it puts a number on the confounding rather than asserting its absence. Negative-control exposures work the same way in reverse: something that could not cause the outcome but shares its confounders.

concept:concept.not_yet_treated.in_more_depth: The obvious comparison group in a staggered design is the units that never adopt. Sometimes there are very few of them, and they are often unusual for the very reason they never adopted. The alternative is to borrow from the future: in 2006 a state that adopts in 2011 is untreated, and it probably resembles a 2007 adopter more closely than a permanent hold-out does. Two costs come with it. The pool thins as the panel runs on and more units switch on, so the later periods rest on fewer comparisons than the early ones. And it assumes those waiting units are not already reacting to a policy they can see coming, which is the no-anticipation assumption doing real work rather than sitting decoratively in the ledger.

concept:concept.placebo.in_more_depth: A placebo outcome is one the treatment should not touch. A placebo treatment is a fake date or a permuted assignment. A placebo unit is a donor treated as though it had been intervened on. Each asks the same question: does this design manufacture findings? A clean placebo is reassuring and not decisive -- it rules out one route to a false positive, not all of them. A dirty placebo is much more informative, because it demonstrates a problem rather than failing to find one.

concept:concept.spec_curve.in_more_depth: A robustness check that reports three alternative specifications is a sample of size three from a space the analyst chose. A specification curve runs the grid -- covariate sets, calipers, bandwidths, trimming thresholds -- and plots all of them with the headline marked. A conclusion that survives most of the curve is stronger than one that survives three hand-picked variants. A curve that swings through zero tells you the finding is a specification, not a result.

concept:concept.staggered_adoption.in_more_depth: With a single adoption date the comparison is easy to state: adopters against non-adopters, before against after. When states adopt in 2004, 2009 and 2013, one regression coefficient has to combine many overlapping comparisons, and some of them treat a unit that is already under the policy as though it were an untreated control. If the effect grows or fades after adoption, those comparisons subtract one real effect from another and can drag the average towards zero, or past it. Estimators built for staggered adoption avoid this by never using an already-treated unit as a control. They compute one effect for each adoption cohort in each period and then average those blocks with weights you can look at and argue with.
concept:concept.staggered_adoption.one_liner: Units switch the policy on at different dates rather than all at once. It is the ordinary case in policy data, and it breaks the simplest before-and-after arithmetic.
concept:concept.staggered_adoption.plain_language: Units switch the policy on at different dates rather than all at once. It is the ordinary case in policy data, and it breaks the simplest before-and-after arithmetic.

concept:concept.standardised_difference.in_more_depth: It is the number a Love plot shows, before and after adjustment. Unlike a t-test of balance, it does not shrink as the sample grows, which is why balance is judged with it rather than with p-values.

concept:concept.target_trial.in_more_depth: Eligibility, time zero, the treatment strategies being compared, the follow-up, the outcome, and the causal contrast. Making each explicit catches most of the errors that produce implausible observational results: immortal time bias, prevalent-user bias, and outcomes that precede the exposure. It is also the fastest way to notice that a question has no well-defined intervention behind it, in which case the estimand needs rewriting before any estimator is chosen.

concept:concept.twfe.in_more_depth: "Fixed effect" here just means a separate intercept. One per unit absorbs everything about a state that never changes -- its size, its politics, its weather. One per period absorbs anything that hit everybody at once, like a recession. What is left to explain the outcome is the timing of the policy. With two groups and two periods this reproduces the difference-in-differences answer exactly. With many adoption dates it no longer does. The single coefficient becomes a weighted average of every two-group, two-period comparison the data allows, including ones that use an early adopter as the control for a later one. Those weights are decided by the arithmetic rather than by you, and some of them can be negative. The decomposition diagnostic shows what your particular number is made of.

concept:guardrail.bad_control.in_more_depth: If a training programme raises earnings partly by raising the chance of being employed, then adjusting for employment removes that pathway from the estimate. The number you get is not the effect of the programme; it is the effect holding fixed one of the ways the programme works. Causal Capybara flags variables that look post-treatment -- by name, and by timing when the design has a time variable -- and marks them on the board. It does not remove them for you: the guardrail explains, and you decide. If you genuinely want the effect that does not run through a mediator, that is a controlled direct effect, and it is a different estimand with its own assumptions.

design:did.in_more_depth: Comparing changes removes anything about a unit that is fixed over time -- you do not need to measure it, only to believe it is stable. That is a real gain, and it is bought with a different assumption: that without the policy the two groups would have moved the same way. When everyone adopts at the same date, this is a clean 2x2. When they adopt at different dates, two-way fixed effects stops estimating what you want: it averages comparisons that include already-treated units acting as controls, with weights that can go negative. The modern estimators fix that by only ever comparing a newly treated cohort with units not yet treated. Clustering matters here more than almost anywhere. Standard errors should be clustered at the level treatment was assigned.

design:its.how_the_board_reads: The counterfactual trend is an assumption, not an estimate.
design:its.in_more_depth: Common in public health, where a rule changes nationally and there is no untreated region. The strength is that the unit is its own control; the weakness is that the counterfactual is entirely a modelling assumption, and an extrapolated linear trend over several years is a strong claim. Three things routinely go wrong. Seasonality left unmodelled shows up as an effect. Autocorrelated residuals make the confidence interval far too narrow. And anything else that changed on the same date is inseparable from the policy -- which is why a control series that should not have been affected is worth a great deal.

design:iv.how_the_board_reads: The arrow from the instrument straight to the outcome is missing on purpose. That missing arrow is the exclusion restriction, and it is an assumption you are making.
design:iv.in_more_depth: The instrument does the work randomisation would have done, but only for part of the population: the compliers, whose treatment status the instrument actually changed. It says nothing about people who would have been treated regardless, or never. The arrow you did not draw -- from instrument straight to outcome -- is the exclusion restriction, and it cannot be tested. A strong first stage tells you the instrument moves treatment; it is silent about other routes. Weak instruments are the practical trap. Below an effective F of about ten, the usual interval is not trustworthy and a weak-instrument-robust set is the honest report, even when it is unbounded.

design:longitudinal.how_the_board_reads: Treatment and confounders both move over time, and each can only be affected by what came before it. Whether a covariate is treated as measured at the same time as the treatment or one period earlier changes the answer, so say which you mean.
design:longitudinal.in_more_depth: This is the setting ordinary regression cannot handle. A variable like blood pressure or employment status is a consequence of past treatment and a cause of future treatment. Adjust for it and you block part of the effect and open a collider path; ignore it and confounding remains. G-methods solve it by modelling the treatment process over time instead of conditioning on its consequences: inverse-probability weighting for a marginal structural model, the parametric g-formula, or a sequential doubly robust estimator. Lag discipline is the practical rule, and the board enforces it: a covariate may adjust a treatment decision only if it was measured before that decision. Arrows cannot point into the past.

design:mediation.how_the_board_reads: You have to believe you measured everything that confounds treatment with the outcome AND everything that confounds the mediator with the outcome. That second half is the hard one, and it is what statisticians call sequential ignorability.
design:mediation.in_more_depth: Mediation needs two exchangeability assumptions rather than one, and the second is harder than the first: even in a randomised trial, the mediator is not randomised, so whatever determines it may also drive the outcome. Natural direct and indirect effects need a third condition comparing outcomes across worlds no person can inhabit at once. It is not testable, even in principle. Interventional effects replace it with something a trial could implement, which is why they are the better default for policy and health questions. Do not start from a product of two regression coefficients. It is only the indirect effect under linearity and no interaction, and it is silent about the assumptions.

design:observational.in_more_depth: This is the workhorse and the hardest design to defend. The estimate is only as good as the adjustment set, and no diagnostic can tell you whether the set is complete -- balance plots only speak about the variables in it. Two things you can do. First, look at overlap: where the treated and untreated groups do not resemble each other at all, no method compares anything, it extrapolates. Second, ask the sensitivity question: how strong would an unmeasured confounder have to be, relative to the ones you did measure, to overturn the finding? Be careful about what goes into the adjustment set. Variables measured after treatment, or caused by it, make things worse rather than better.

design:rct.in_more_depth: What randomisation buys you is exchangeability for free. What it does not buy you is everything afterwards: people drop out, refuse the treatment, or take it when they were not offered it, and each of those can undo the comparison. So the questions this design asks are about implementation. Was assignment really random, or did someone with discretion do it? Did whole clusters get assigned together, in which case the number of independent observations is the number of clusters? Did everyone offered the programme take it, and if not, is the number you want the effect of the offer or the effect on the people it moved? Covariates are for precision here, not identification. Adjust for the ones you named before seeing the data.

design:rd.how_the_board_reads: Type the threshold into the Cutoff box. The binned scatter appears before any estimator does.
design:rd.in_more_depth: The credibility of this design is local and its estimate is local with it. You learn about units at the cutoff and nobody else, which is exactly right if the policy question is about moving the threshold, and a poor fit if it is about the programme overall. Two things can break it. If people could control their score precisely, they sorted across the line and the comparison is not as-good-as-random -- the density test looks for that. If the same threshold triggers other rules, the jump combines them and nothing separates them. The binned scatter is the design. If you cannot see the discontinuity, be suspicious of an estimator that reports one.

design:synth.how_the_board_reads: If the synthetic unit cannot reproduce the pre-period, it is not a counterfactual.
design:synth.in_more_depth: This is what you reach for when the treated unit is a country, a region or a firm, and there is no comparable single control. The weights are chosen to reproduce the pre-intervention path, and the restriction that they are non-negative and sum to one is deliberate: it forbids extrapolation. Pre-period fit is the test. A synthetic unit that cannot reproduce the treated unit before the intervention has no claim to reproduce it afterwards, and the estimate is then mostly the pre-existing gap. Inference is by permutation, not by standard errors: re-run the method pretending each donor was treated, and see where the real one ranks.

design:synth.plain_language: One treated unit, many untreated donors. Build a weighted combination of donors that tracks the treated unit before the intervention, and use it afterwards.

probes.one_liner: Simulate a common cause of a stated strength and watch the estimate move; read off how strong one would have to be to explain the result away.
probes.title: Unobserved confounder

probes.one_liner: Run the grid of defensible specifications and sort the answers. The curve is the result, not the one you happened to run.

probes.one_liner: Drop one cluster, cohort or donor at a time and see whether any single one is carrying the result.
probes.title: Leave one out

probes.one_liner: Estimate something that shares the confounding but not the causal path. A non-zero answer is bias you can see.
probes.title: Negative control

probes.one_liner: Run the same analysis on something the treatment could not have changed. It should find nothing.
probes.title: Placebo outcome

probes.one_liner: Move the policy date earlier, reshuffle who was treated, or swap in a variable that cannot cause the outcome.
probes.title: Placebo treatment

probes.one_liner: Add a variable that causes nothing to the adjustment set. The estimate should barely move.
probes.title: Random common cause

probes.one_liner: Re-estimate on random subsets. The answer should move about as much as losing that much data costs, and no more.
probes.title: Subset stability

diagnostic:adoption.in_more_depth: This is the picture that decides which difference-in-differences estimator you should be using. A single block of lit cells starting at one date is a 2x2. A staircase is staggered adoption, and two-way fixed effects is then averaging comparisons that include already-treated units used as controls. It also shows what you have to compare against: a row of never-treated units at the bottom, or nothing, in which case the comparison group has to be units not yet treated.

diagnostic:augmentation_gap.in_more_depth: Doubly robust methods combine a model of the outcome with a model of the treatment, and are consistent if either one is right. The correction term is the part that makes that guarantee work. Its size measures how much the two models disagree about the same data. A small gap means both models tell the same story and the guarantee is not being exercised. A large one means they do not, and the estimate is relying on the promise that at least one of them is right -- a promise that cannot be checked.
diagnostic:augmentation_gap.one_liner: The distance between the plain model-based estimate and the version with a correction term added.
diagnostic:augmentation_gap.plain_language: The distance between the plain model-based estimate and the version with a correction term added.

diagnostic:bacon_decomposition.in_more_depth: When units adopt a policy at different dates, a two-way fixed-effects regression is not one comparison; it is an average of many two-group, two-period comparisons. Some of them are the ones you would want: a group that adopts against a group that never does. Others compare a late adopter against an early adopter who is already treated -- using treated units as the control group. Those latter comparisons subtract the early group's ongoing effect, so if effects grow over time they can push the average in the wrong direction, and the weight attached to them can even be negative. This decomposition shows how much of your number comes from each kind, which is the evidence for whether a modern estimator is needed.
diagnostic:bacon_decomposition.one_liner: Every simple before-and-after comparison hidden inside a single fixed-effects coefficient, and how much weight each one carries.

diagnostic:bandwidth_sensitivity.in_more_depth: Every discontinuity estimate is a choice about how far from the threshold to look. Narrow windows use only the most comparable units and are noisy; wide ones are precise and rely on the fitted curve to describe a longer stretch of the relationship. Automatic selectors trade the two off, and reasonable selectors disagree with each other. A finding that persists across a range of windows is much stronger than one that appears at the selected width and disappears either side. This path is how you tell which you have.
diagnostic:bandwidth_sensitivity.one_liner: The estimate recomputed using progressively wider and narrower windows around the cutoff.

diagnostic:baseline_balance.in_more_depth: Randomisation makes the arms comparable in expectation, not in every sample. The balance table is a check on the mechanics: that the randomiser worked, that nobody was reassigned, that the data was not merged wrongly. It is not a test of whether randomisation "worked" in a deeper sense. With many covariates some will differ by chance, and adjusting for whichever ones came out significant is a forking path, not a repair. Pre-specified covariate adjustment for precision is a different and better idea.

diagnostic:bias_correction.in_more_depth: The window width that gives the most accurate estimate is deliberately a little too wide -- it accepts some bias in exchange for a lot less noise. That trade means the leftover bias is about the same size as the standard error, so an interval computed as though there were none is too narrow and sits slightly off-centre. The remedy is to estimate the bias with a more flexible fit, subtract it, and widen the interval to account for having estimated it. The corrected interval is wider on purpose. It is the honest one at a window chosen for accuracy.
diagnostic:bias_correction.one_liner: Fitting a curve over a window leaves a predictable error at the edge. This shows how much correcting for it moves the estimate and widens the interval.

diagnostic:block_structure.in_more_depth: A blocked trial is many small trials stacked together, and the analysis has to respect that: comparisons are made inside blocks and then averaged. This table is how you check the stacking is sound. Blocks that hold only treated units, or only untreated ones, contain no comparison and are dropped, and the table says how many were lost that way. Block sizes also decide how the interval is computed. With two units in a block there is no spread to measure inside it, so the calculation falls back on pooling across blocks, which assumes the blocks behave alike. That is a real assumption and it is worth knowing when you are leaning on it.
diagnostic:block_structure.one_liner: When randomisation was done separately inside strata -- clinics, schools, waves -- this shows how big each block is and what share of it was treated.

diagnostic:block_weighting.in_more_depth: Averaging the block-level effects with each block weighted by how many units it holds gives the average effect across everyone in the study. Putting an indicator variable in for each block instead gives a precision-weighted average: it leans on the blocks where the treated share is nearest a half, because those blocks carry the most information. The two agree only when the treated share is the same in every block. Neither is wrong. But if you asked for the average effect on this population, the size-weighted number is the one that answers it, and the regression coefficient is quietly answering a different question under the same name.
diagnostic:block_weighting.one_liner: Two ways of combining blocked results give two different numbers, and the difference is a difference in the question, not in the arithmetic.

diagnostic:bootstrap_spread.in_more_depth: Resampling the data with replacement and repeating the entire fit -- models and all -- gives a picture of how much the answer would move if you had drawn a different sample from the same population. It is the fallback when no formula for the standard error is trustworthy, which is often the case once weights have been estimated rather than known. Two things are worth reading here rather than just the interval. First, how many resamples failed: a fit that breaks on some draws is telling you the model is fragile. Second, the shape: two humps mean the models are not fitting the same way on every resample, and an average of two behaviours is not a summary of either.
diagnostic:bootstrap_spread.one_liner: The whole estimate recomputed on many resamples of the data, and whether those resamples behaved themselves.
diagnostic:bootstrap_spread.plain_language: The whole estimate recomputed on many resamples of the data, and whether those resamples behaved themselves.

diagnostic:cate_calibration.in_more_depth: A model will always produce varying predictions, including from pure noise. Calibration asks whether the ranking means anything: regress the realised effect on the predicted one, and see whether the slope is near one. A slope near zero says the heterogeneity is a model artefact. This is the check that separates "we found who benefits" from "we fitted a forest".

diagnostic:cde_path.in_more_depth: A controlled direct effect asks what the treatment would do if the mediator were fixed, by intervention, at a particular level for everybody. diagnostic:censoring_weights.in_more_depth: People drop out, and if they drop out for reasons connected to their treatment or their outcome, the ones who remain are a selected group. The standard repair is to model who stays and then let each person who stayed stand in for the similar people who left. That works only if staying is predictable from what was measured. It also has the same failure mode as any weighting: when few people like someone remained, that person's weight becomes large and the estimate leans on them. The range of weights reported here is how you see it happening.

diagnostic:compliance.in_more_depth: Offering a programme is not the same as delivering it. Some people offered it decline; some people not offered it find it anyway. The gap in take-up between the arms is what the analysis divides by when it converts the effect of the offer into the effect of the treatment, so a small gap means dividing by a small number, and the interval widens fast. That same gap defines who the number describes. Provided the offer never pushed anybody away from treatment, the people whose take-up the offer actually changed are the compliers, and the estimate is their effect -- not the effect for the people who would have taken it up regardless, nor for those who never would, nor for the population as a whole.

diagnostic:compliers.in_more_depth: Divide the sample into three kinds. Some would take the treatment whatever happened. Some would never take it. The rest -- the ones the instrument actually moves -- are the only people the estimate describes. Their share can be worked out from the take-up rates in each group, provided the instrument never pushed anybody in the wrong direction. A small share is not a flaw in the arithmetic, but it does limit the claim. An estimate for eight per cent of the sample is an estimate for eight per cent of the sample, and there is no statistical route from there to everybody else.

diagnostic:constant_effect.in_more_depth: The partially linear model writes the outcome as one effect multiplied by the treatment, plus a flexible function of the confounders. The flexibility is all on the confounding side; the effect itself is a single number by construction. That restriction makes the estimator efficient and simple. When effects really do differ between people, the number it returns is a weighted average that leans towards the units whose treatment was hardest to predict. That is not the average treatment effect, though it is often close. If the heterogeneity checks find real differences, use the estimator that targets the average directly instead.

diagnostic:differential_attrition.in_more_depth: Randomisation makes the arms comparable at the moment of assignment. It says nothing about who is still in the file at the end. If the people offered the programme are more likely to answer the follow-up survey -- or less likely -- then the sample being compared has been selected by something that happened after assignment, and the protection randomisation bought you is gone. Adjusting for baseline characteristics does not repair this, because the selection happened downstream of the treatment rather than before it. What helps is bounding the answer under best and worst cases for the missing rows, and reporting the loss plainly.

diagnostic:ebal_convergence.in_more_depth: Entropy balancing does not fit a model of treatment and hope for balance; it solves directly for weights that make named summaries of the covariates -- means, and optionally spreads -- match between the groups exactly. When a solution exists, the remaining gaps are zero by construction and this table is a receipt. When no solution exists, the gaps are not zero, and that is informative: it means the treated group's profile is outside anything a reweighting of the available comparison units can reproduce. That is a data problem, not a solver problem, and no amount of tuning fixes it.

diagnostic:endogeneity.in_more_depth: The two numbers are not competing estimates of the same thing. The plain regression describes an association across everybody; the instrumented figure is a causal effect for the people the instrument moves. They can differ because of confounding, because those people are unusual, or both. A formal test of whether the plain regression would have been enough exists and is reported, but it is only meaningful if the instrument is valid and strong. When the instrument is weak, a large gap between the two numbers is exactly what weak-instrument bias produces, so the gap is not evidence of confounding.

diagnostic:evalue.in_more_depth: An E-value of 2.5 means a hidden variable would have to be associated with both the treatment and the outcome by a risk ratio of at least 2.5, above and beyond the covariates already in the model, before the finding could be attributed to it entirely. The same calculation applied to the end of the confidence interval says what it would take to move the result to the edge of statistical significance rather than to nothing. It is a convenient summary and it is not a test. It says nothing about whether such a variable exists, and it assumes a single confounder acting simply. Its value comes from the comparison with the associations your measured covariates actually show.

diagnostic:evalue_scale.in_more_depth: A difference in means, an odds ratio, a hazard ratio: each needs a different bridge to the risk-ratio scale the E-value formula expects, and each bridge carries its own conditions. Converting an odds ratio assumes the outcome is rare. Converting a standardised mean difference assumes the outcome is roughly bell-shaped. Where those conditions fail, the E-value inherits the failure. This row records which conversion was used, so that a reader can judge it rather than take the resulting number at face value.

diagnostic:extreme_confounder.in_more_depth: This is the worst case for one half of the problem and therefore a useful bound. By granting the hidden variable complete command of the treatment assignment, the question reduces to a single quantity: how strongly it would have to relate to the outcome to move the estimate to zero. If that remaining requirement is large, the finding survives even the most adverse assumption about selection into treatment. If it is small, then even a mild relationship with the outcome would suffice, and the estimate should be described as fragile.

diagnostic:forest_honesty.in_more_depth: If the same rows both choose a split and estimate the effect on either side of it, the effect will look large -- the split was chosen because it looked large. Honest forests avoid that by dividing each tree's sample in two: one half draws the boundaries, the other half fills in the numbers, and no unit contributes to both jobs in the same tree. Each unit's own predicted effect then comes only from trees that never saw it. The cost is sample size, and this panel reports what that cost was: leaves too sparse to estimate, and units with few trees to average over, both push the per-person predictions back towards the overall average.

diagnostic:honest_did.in_more_depth: A pre-trend test that fails to reject is weak evidence, because such tests have little power exactly when a violation would matter. The alternative is to allow the trends to differ by some amount after treatment, widen the interval accordingly, and report the largest violation the conclusion can absorb. That number is called a breakdown value. Expressed in relative terms, it says how big a post-treatment violation would have to be compared with the wobbles already visible before treatment. It is a much more useful summary than a yes-or-no test, and it is still an assumption -- about the class of violations considered, not about their absence.

diagnostic:icc_design_effect.in_more_depth: Two pupils in one school resemble each other more than two pupils picked at random from the country, and the intracluster correlation puts a number between zero and one on that resemblance. Combine it with the cluster sizes and you get the design effect: the factor by which the sample behaves smaller than it looks. A design effect of four means a thousand rows carry about two hundred and fifty observations' worth of information. This is not a fault to be repaired. It is the price of assigning treatment to groups, and it should have been in the sample-size calculation before the study ran.

If the untreated cells are not well described by unit and period effects alone, the predicted counterfactual carries error that lands entirely in the estimate.

diagnostic:influence_spread.in_more_depth: Most modern estimators can be written as an average of one number per unit, and the standard error is the spread of those numbers divided by the sample size. diagnostic:its_autocorrelation.in_more_depth: Monthly and quarterly series are almost always autocorrelated: a busy month is followed by a busy month. Ignoring it does not bias the estimate much but it shrinks the standard error, sometimes by a factor of two or three, which turns noise into a finding. The autocorrelation function of the residuals and a Ljung-Box test are the standard checks. When they fire, use a HAC standard error or model the error process explicitly, and say which in the report.

diagnostic:its_control_shock.in_more_depth: The weakness of a single interrupted series is that anything else happening at the same time is indistinguishable from the policy. A control series -- a neighbouring region, an unaffected condition, an untargeted product -- turns that from an assumption into something partly checkable. If the control jumps at the same date in the same direction, the change was not the policy. If the two series were already drifting apart beforehand, the control was not a good stand-in to begin with, and the comparison inherits the drift.

diagnostic:its_model_choice.in_more_depth: Time-series models differ in how they treat the series' memory -- whether today's value depends on yesterday's, on the surprise in yesterday's, or on the trend needing removal before either. Automatic selection picks the model that scores best on a fit criterion, and often several candidates score almost the same. When they do, the choice is close to arbitrary and it can matter for the estimate. Whether that is visible here decides how much the modelling can be trusted; a model can always fit a step, and this is where you find out whether there is one to fit. Three things are worth checking. diagnostic:leave_one_out.in_more_depth: An estimate that survives dropping any single unit is about a population. An estimate that collapses when one row leaves is about that row. This check does not need a model of anything; it just re-runs the analysis with each unit held out and plots where the answers land. It matters most when the number of units doing the work is small: a synthetic control built from a handful of donors, a panel with few clusters, or a matched analysis where one comparison unit was reused many times.

diagnostic:level_jump_at_kink.in_more_depth: Where a benefit formula changes its rate at a threshold, the design reads the change in slope as the effect. That reading requires the level itself to be continuous: if crossing the threshold also delivers a lump sum, or switches on some other entitlement, then a step and a bend are both present and attributing everything to the bend is wrong. The test fits a step in the same window. Finding one does not invalidate the data; it means the threshold does two things, and both should be estimated.

diagnostic:love.in_more_depth: Named after Thomas Love. Each covariate contributes one point before adjustment and one after, so you can see at a glance whether matching or weighting achieved what it promised. The dashed line at 0.1 is a convention. What matters is whether a residual imbalance sits on a variable that strongly predicts the outcome; a large remaining difference on an irrelevant covariate is harmless, and a small one on a powerful predictor is not. Variance ratios are reported alongside: two groups can have the same mean and very different spread, and matching on means alone will not show it.

diagnostic:manipulation.in_more_depth: The design works because units just either side of the threshold are otherwise alike -- an accident of a decimal place decided who got the programme. That stops being true if people could see the threshold and move themselves across it, because the ones who managed it are precisely those who wanted the treatment most or had the resources to arrange it. The check is a comparison of how densely packed the units are on each side. A smooth transition does not prove nobody manipulated anything; a visible cliff is strong evidence that somebody did.

diagnostic:mediation_decomposition.in_more_depth: The split is arithmetic: the two parts add to the total by construction, so their adding up is not evidence that either is right. Both pieces rest on the assumption that nothing unmeasured confounds the mediator and the outcome, which is usually harder to defend than the assumption about the treatment itself -- randomising a programme does not randomise how much of it people take up. The proportion mediated is the most-quoted and least-reliable summary here. It is a ratio of two estimates, it is unstable when the total effect is small, and it is not a share of anything at all when the two parts have opposite signs.

diagnostic:metalearner_plug_in.in_more_depth: Flexible learners are deliberately cautious: they pull predictions towards the middle to avoid fitting noise. That shrinkage is what makes them good at ranking people, and it is exactly what makes their average a poor estimate of the average effect -- the bias does not cancel out when you average, and no standard error is available for it. So the two numbers do different jobs. Use the per-person predictions to decide who to prioritise; use the headline, which is built to have a valid interval, to say how large the effect is.

diagnostic:multiple_mediators.in_more_depth: Shifting each mediator on its own and then shifting them together gives three numbers, and the single-mediator effects will generally not sum to the joint one. The difference is what the mediators do jointly -- through interacting with each other, or because one causes another -- and it cannot be assigned to either of them. Pathway effects therefore partition the total only when the mediators neither interact nor cause one another, which is a strong condition and rarely stated when such tables are published.

diagnostic:natural_course.in_more_depth: Simulation-based methods answer questions by generating fictional worlds from fitted models -- everybody treated, nobody treated, treated under some rule. The one world that can be checked is the one that already happened: let the simulation draw treatment from the fitted model instead of setting it by hand, and the result should look like the observed data. This is the only check on the models these methods depend on. Passing it does not make the intervened worlds correct, since those extrapolate beyond what was observed, but failing it means the machinery is misdescribing even the world it was fitted to.

diagnostic:negative_control.in_more_depth: Choose something that shares the same confounding as your real outcome but that the treatment could not touch -- an event before treatment began, or an unrelated condition. If people who took the treatment also do better on that, the difference cannot be the treatment, so it is whatever else separates the groups. This is more useful than any balance table, because it puts a number on the confounding rather than asserting its absence. A clean negative control is reassuring but not decisive: it rules out one route to a false positive, not all of them.

diagnostic:nuisance_rmse.in_more_depth: Double machine learning is only as good as its cross-fitting. These numbers tell you whether the nuisance models are learning anything, and whether they are stable: an out-of-fold error that swings wildly means the answer depends on which rows landed where. They are not model-selection criteria. A better-predicting nuisance model does not automatically give a better causal estimate; orthogonality is what protects the estimate, and these diagnostics tell you whether the machinery behind it is behaving.

diagnostic:oster_assumptions.in_more_depth: The first is proportional selection: the variables you did not measure are related to the treatment in the same proportion as the ones you did. That would be true if your controls were a random draw from all possible confounders, and they almost never are -- researchers measure what they suspect matters. The second is a value for how well a regression including everything would fit the outcome. It is assumed rather than estimated, usually as a multiple of the fit you achieved, and the bound is sensitive to the choice. Both assumptions are reported here so the bound can be read as the conditional statement it is.
diagnostic:oster_assumptions.one_liner: The two assumptions behind the delta figure, stated plainly, because the number is meaningless without them.

diagnostic:oster_delta.in_more_depth: The idea starts from something you can watch: how far the estimate moves when you add your control variables, and how much better the model fits once they are in. If adding controls barely moves the estimate but greatly improves the fit, the controls were informative and yet unimportant to the answer -- which is mild evidence that further controls would behave the same way. Delta turns that reasoning into a number. Read it with care. The calculation needs an assumption about how well a regression on absolutely everything would fit, and nothing in your data pins that down; the bound moves a long way as you change it.

diagnostic:outcome_distribution.in_more_depth: A difference in means is a summary, and summaries hide things. An outcome piled up at zero, a count with a long tail, or a scale where almost everybody gives the same answer will each produce a mean difference, and in each case the mean difference is a poor description of what the treatment did. Look at the shape first. It tells you whether a straight-line model is a reasonable working description, whether the effect might sit at one end of the distribution rather than in the middle, and whether a transformation would change the question you are answering rather than just the units it is answered in.

diagnostic:overlap.in_more_depth: Fit a model for the probability of being treated given the covariates, then plot the fitted probabilities by arm. If treated units sit at values no control unit reaches, the estimate for those units is produced by extrapolating the outcome model rather than by comparing anything. Both matter: a picture can look reasonable while the effective sample has collapsed.

diagnostic:panel_balance.in_more_depth: Fixed effects compare a unit with itself over time, which works when the unit is there throughout. Units that appear or disappear mid-panel change the composition of the average, and if they do so around the time treatment arrives, the change in the average is partly a change in who is being averaged. That is selection, not bookkeeping, and no fixed effect removes it. The honest responses are to restrict to a balanced set of units and see whether the answer moves, or to model the entry and exit explicitly.

diagnostic:permutation_distribution.in_more_depth: This is inference that borrows nothing from the bell curve. If the treatment did nothing at all to anybody, then any relabelling of who was treated was equally likely, and the estimate you got should look like a typical draw from the reshuffled ones. The p-value is the share of reshuffles that came out at least as extreme as the real result. The reshuffling has to imitate the real assignment -- inside blocks, whole clusters at a time -- or it is answering a question about a study that was never run. Note also what is being tested: the sharp null that treatment changed nothing for anyone, which is a stronger statement than the usual null that the average effect is zero.
diagnostic:permutation_distribution.one_liner: Reshuffle the treatment labels the way the study actually assigned them, thousands of times, and see how unusual the real result looks.
diagnostic:permutation_distribution.plain_language: Reshuffle the treatment labels the way the study actually assigned them, thousands of times, and see how unusual the real result looks.

produced_by.one_liner: Re-run the randomisation thousands of times with the outcomes held fixed, and see how unusual what actually happened really is.

diagnostic:person_time.in_more_depth: Methods for treatment that changes over time learn from people whose treatment changes. If almost everybody is either always treated or never treated, there is very little switching to learn from, and the machinery built for time-varying treatment has nothing much to work with. The count of distinct histories is the honest measure of that. It is also the reason these analyses need more data than they appear to: the effective sample is the number of people whose history differs, not the number of person-period rows.

diagnostic:placebo_outcome.in_more_depth: The logic is the same as a negative control and the emphasis is different: here the point is to test the design as a whole -- the comparison group, the timing, the adjustment -- rather than to measure confounding specifically. A placebo effect of the same size and sign as the headline is a serious problem, because whatever produced it is presumably also present in the real outcome. A null placebo is worth reporting and is weak evidence: it shows the design did not fail in this particular way.

diagnostic:placebo_reduced_form.in_more_depth: The design requires the instrument to reach the outcome only through the treatment. That cannot be proved, but it can be caught failing: pick outcomes the treatment could not plausibly affect, and see whether the instrument moves them. If it does, there is a second route out of the instrument, and the exclusion restriction is not holding. Nothing moving is worth reporting and is not proof. It narrows the space of violations rather than closing it.

diagnostic:placebo_treatment.in_more_depth: A fake treatment has no effect by construction, so anything the analysis reports for it is coming from somewhere else: a trend the design does not handle, a comparison group that was never comparable, or a model flexible enough to fit noise. diagnostic:policy_value.in_more_depth: A rule learned from data always looks good on that same data. The only honest valuation holds part of the sample back, applies the finished rule to it, and scores what it would have achieved there. That is the number to quote. The comparison that matters is not against treating nobody but against treating everybody, since blanket treatment is usually simpler to run and easier to defend. If the gain over treating everybody has an interval that includes zero, targeting has not been shown to be worth its complexity. Note the interval holds the fitted models fixed, so it is slightly narrower than the truth.

diagnostic:positivity_by_period.in_more_depth: Overlap is harder over time than at a single point, because it has to hold at each period and for each history. Once a patient has been on a drug for three periods, almost everybody like them stays on it, and the analysis is then asking what would have happened had they stopped -- a question the data contains no example of. This panel reports the worst period rather than the average, because positivity has to hold everywhere. A single period where treatment is nearly certain contaminates every quantity computed across the whole follow-up.

diagnostic:pre_trends.in_more_depth: Failing to reject is not confirmation. Pre-trend tests often have low power precisely in the situations where a violation would matter, and conditioning the analysis on having passed one distorts the estimates that follow. That produces a breakdown value rather than a verdict.

diagnostic:probe_runs.in_more_depth: A probe such as a placebo test or a specification curve works by running the whole analysis again under changed conditions. Some of those runs fail: a model does not converge, a subsample has nobody in one arm, a bandwidth leaves too few observations. Failures are not neutral and they are not noise. The specifications that could not be estimated are often the demanding ones, so a probe that only reports its successes is quietly reporting the easy half. This row exists so the count is visible next to the conclusion drawn from it.

diagnostic:propensity_clipping.in_more_depth: Inverse-probability weighting divides by the estimated chance of getting the treatment you actually got. When that chance is 0.001 the weight is a thousand, and one row swamps everything. The standard defence is clipping: pull extreme probabilities back to a floor and a ceiling before the division. Clipping stabilises the arithmetic and quietly changes the question. The units at the clip are the ones with no counterpart in the other arm, so keeping them at a fictitious probability is a modelling choice, not a measurement. Whichever way you go, the honest report says how many units were clipped and where the boundaries were set.
diagnostic:propensity_clipping.one_liner: How many units had an estimated chance of treatment so close to zero or one that the analysis had to trim it back before dividing by it.

diagnostic:random_common_cause.in_more_depth: This is a check on the machinery rather than on the design. A variable generated at random causes nothing and is caused by nothing, so including it should leave the estimate essentially where it was, give or take a little sampling noise. When the estimate does move, the adjustment is unstable -- typically because the model is straining against thin overlap, or has more parameters than the data can support. Passing this check is reassuring about the arithmetic and says nothing whatever about unmeasured confounding.

diagnostic:raw_means.in_more_depth: This is the picture the whole design argues about. Difference-in-differences claims that, absent the policy, the treated group's line would have continued parallel to the comparison group's. You cannot check that claim after treatment, but you can look at the lines before it, and you can see whether they were the same shape. Everything the estimator does afterwards is a subtraction on these averages. If the lines look wrong here -- crossing, diverging, one of them jumping in a period when nothing happened to it -- no fixed effect further down the pipeline will repair that.

diagnostic:rd_plot.in_more_depth: This plot is the design. Before any technical choice has been made, it shows whether something happens at the threshold and whether the relationship away from the threshold is smooth enough for a local fit to be believable. The step you can see in the fitted curve at the cutoff is the estimate; nothing else in the analysis adds a jump that is not visible here. diagnostic:reduced_form.in_more_depth: If the instrument was well assigned, its relationship with the outcome is itself a credible causal effect -- of the encouragement, not of the treatment. That makes it the sturdiest number in an instrumental-variables analysis: no division, no weak-instrument problem, no reliance on how many people the instrument moved. A flat reduced form is decisive in a way the ratio is not. If the encouragement did not move the outcome at all, then either the treatment does nothing or the encouragement did not move treatment, and the ratio of two small numbers will not settle which.

diagnostic:robustness_value.in_more_depth: The robustness value is expressed as a share of the variation left over after your controls: a value of 0.05 means a hidden variable explaining five per cent of the remaining variation in treatment and five per cent of the remaining variation in the outcome would be enough to erase the estimate. Its usefulness comes from the benchmark. The same quantity can be computed for the covariates you did measure, so you can say "an unmeasured variable would have to be twice as informative as household income" instead of quoting an abstract number. Note the calculation assumes the hidden variable enters linearly and on its own, so it is a guide, not a guarantee.

diagnostic:rosenbaum_bounds.in_more_depth: Matching pairs units that look alike on the variables you measured. If something you did not measure still made one of them more likely to be treated, the pair is not the fair comparison it appears to be. The bound asks how large that hidden difference in the odds of treatment would have to be -- a factor of 1.2, of 2, of 5 -- before the result could be explained by it. The number is often called Gamma. It is a statement about a comparison, not a discovery about the world: it does not say a hidden variable exists, only what one would have to do. Note too that it assumes the hidden variable affects treatment but is otherwise summarised by that single factor.

diagnostic:running_variable_discreteness.in_more_depth: The usual analysis treats the score as continuous, so that units get arbitrarily close to the threshold from both sides. Scores that take only whole numbers, or only a few values, break that picture: there is a nearest value below and a nearest value above, and nothing in between. When that happens the honest treatment is different. Standard errors should allow for units sharing a value, and an analysis that treats the units at the two adjacent values as if they had been randomised fits the situation better than a curve fitted through a handful of points.

diagnostic:sc_augmentation.in_more_depth: When no blend of comparison places can match the treated place, the augmented method estimates the leftover imbalance and corrects for it, using a fitted model to bridge the gap. This is a deliberate, well-motivated extrapolation, and its size tells you how much of the final answer comes from the model rather than from the comparison. A small correction means the donors were nearly good enough and the correction is a refinement. A large one means the pool was inadequate and the answer is substantially a model's prediction.

diagnostic:sc_convex_hull.in_more_depth: A blend with non-negative weights can only land somewhere between the units being blended. If the treated place is more extreme than every comparison place on some characteristic -- richer than all of them, larger than all of them -- then no blend can match it, and the fit will be systematically off in a direction the weights cannot fix. Classic synthetic control refuses to extrapolate and simply fits as best it can. Methods that add a correction term extrapolate deliberately, which is a reasonable response provided the correction is reported and read, not buried.

diagnostic:sc_gap.in_more_depth: Before the intervention the gap should hover near zero -- that is what the weights were chosen to achieve. Afterwards it is free to move, and the movement is the estimated effect. Reading it as a picture rather than as a single number tells you whether the effect arrived suddenly, built up, or faded. The most informative part is often the last stretch before the intervention. A gap that has already started drifting in the direction of the effect indicates anticipation, a mis-dated intervention, or a fit that was never good, and each of those undermines what follows.

diagnostic:sc_mc_rank.in_more_depth: Matrix completion fills in the outcomes that would have been observed if nobody had been treated, by assuming the panel is driven by a small number of underlying patterns shared across units and periods. The rank is how many such patterns were used, and the penalty is what stopped it using more. A higher rank fits the observed data more closely, including its noise. That is why the pre-treatment fit here is not evidence of anything on its own -- the model was fitted on those very periods. The placebo-in-time check is the honest fit test for this family of methods.

diagnostic:sc_placebo_space.in_more_depth: With a single treated unit there is no sampling distribution to appeal to, so the yardstick has to be built by pretending. Each comparison place takes a turn as the treated unit and gets its own gap; the real one is then ranked among them. The statistic is usually the post-intervention gap relative to the pre-intervention fit error, because a place that was fitted badly to begin with will show a large gap afterwards for no interesting reason. Note the arithmetic limit: with seventeen comparison places the smallest attainable p-value is about one in eighteen, which is a property of the design and not a shortcoming of the software.
diagnostic:sc_placebo_space.one_liner: Re-run the whole method pretending each comparison place was the treated one. If many of them show a gap as large, the real one is unremarkable.

diagnostic:sc_placebo_time.in_more_depth: This is the cleanest test of whether the method manufactures breaks. Only data from before the real intervention is used, so any apparent effect at the fake date is produced by the fitting rather than by a policy. A large pseudo-effect means either that the pre-period fit is unstable or that the outcome contains breaks of this size routinely, in which case the real one is not distinguishable from them. It needs enough pre-treatment history to be possible at all, which is why it is sometimes unavailable.

diagnostic:sc_pre_fit.in_more_depth: A synthetic control is a made-up comparison unit: a weighted blend of other places chosen so that the blend follows the treated place through the years before anything happened. If the blend does that well, it is reasonable to let it stand in for what would have happened afterwards. If it does not, there is no argument left. The fit is reported as the typical distance between the two lines before treatment, compared against how much the treated place's own outcome moves about. When that distance is a large share of the outcome's ordinary variation, much of the gap you see afterwards could simply be the same fit error continuing.

diagnostic:sc_weights.in_more_depth: The method chooses a weighted average of the available comparison units, usually with the weights adding to one and none of them negative, so that the result is a genuine blend rather than an extrapolation. Reading the weights is how you sanity-check the comparison: a synthetic California made mostly of two states is a two-state comparison, and those two states' histories are now your identifying assumption.
