what_it_assumes.explains: Assignment really was by chance, and nothing after assignment broke the comparison -- no differential dropout, no crossover you have not modelled.
what_it_assumes.title: Randomisation held
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Dropout differs across arms; take-up is far from assignment; the randomiser was a person with discretion.

what_it_assumes.explains: One unit's treatment does not change another unit's outcome, and "treated" means the same thing for everyone who got it.
what_it_assumes.title: SUTVA / no interference
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Units interact: they compete for the same jobs, infect each other, share a classroom or a market. Or the "programme" is really a family of programmes whose intensity varied a lot across sites.

what_it_assumes.explains: The outcome you observe under the treatment a unit received is the same as the potential outcome under that treatment. In practice: the treatment has to be a thing someone could actually do.
what_it_assumes.title: Consistency / well-defined intervention
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The treatment is a state of the world rather than an action, or it is coded from several very different real interventions.

what_it_assumes.explains: Treated and untreated units are comparable once you condition on the confounders you measured. Everything that pushed people towards treatment and also moves the outcome is in your adjustment set.
what_it_assumes.title: Exchangeability / no unmeasured confounding
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Treatment was chosen by people who knew something about the likely outcome that you do not observe. Clinical judgement, self-selection into a programme, and administrative triage are the classic cases.

what_it_assumes.explains: Every kind of unit had some chance of being treated and some chance of not being treated. Where that fails, there is no comparison to make and the model is inventing one.
what_it_assumes.title: Positivity / overlap
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Any single weight carries a large share of the total; the effective sample is far below the nominal one; the propensity model separates the arms almost perfectly; treated units sit outside the control group's range.

what_it_assumes.explains: Without the policy, treated and comparison groups would have moved the same way. Not that they were at the same level -- that their paths would have been parallel.
what_it_assumes.title: Parallel trends
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Pre-period event-study coefficients drift away from zero; the policy was adopted because outcomes were already moving; the groups differ in composition in ways that interact with time.

what_it_assumes.explains: Units did not change behaviour before treatment arrived because they knew it was coming.
what_it_assumes.title: No anticipation
what_it_assumes.worry_when: There was a public announcement well before the policy started, or the pre-period coefficients move in the period immediately before adoption.

what_it_assumes.explains: People could not precisely control which side of the cutoff they landed on.
what_it_assumes.title: No manipulation of the running variable
what_it_assumes.worry_when: A visible spike or gap in the density at the cutoff; covariates that jump; a cutoff that people knew about and had time to respond to.

what_it_assumes.explains: Everything else that affects the outcome changes smoothly through the cutoff, so the only thing that jumps is the treatment.
what_it_assumes.title: Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Several rules share the threshold; the running variable is coarse, so "at the cutoff" is really a wide band; the estimate depends heavily on the bandwidth.

what_it_assumes.explains: The instrument actually moves treatment, and moves it enough that the resulting estimate is not mostly noise.
what_it_assumes.title: Instrument relevance
what_it_assumes.worry_when: An effective F below about 10; a first-stage coefficient that is substantively tiny even if statistically significant; many instruments.

what_it_assumes.explains: The instrument affects the outcome only through the treatment. On the board, that is the arrow you did not draw.
what_it_assumes.title: Exclusion restriction
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The instrument is a policy that changed several things at once; it is correlated with geography, time or institutions that have their own effects; it was chosen because it predicted the outcome.

what_it_assumes.explains: The instrument pushes everyone the same way, or not at all. Nobody takes the treatment only because they were discouraged from it.
what_it_assumes.title: Monotonicity / no defiers
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The instrument is an incentive that could plausibly backfire for some people, or it is a judge or examiner whose leniency ordering differs across case types.

what_it_assumes.explains: The weighted combination of untreated units reproduces the treated unit's pre-period path closely enough to stand in for it afterwards.
what_it_assumes.title: Pre-treatment fit from the donor pool
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Visible pre-period gaps; a short pre-period relative to the number of donors; one donor carrying most of the weight.

what_it_assumes.explains: The treated unit's characteristics can be written as a weighted average of the donors', with weights that do not go negative.
what_it_assumes.title: Treated unit inside the donor convex hull
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The treated unit is at an extreme of the donor distribution on the predictors, or the pre-period gap has a persistent level offset.

what_it_assumes.explains: Nothing else changed at the same moment that also moves the outcome.
what_it_assumes.title: No co-interventions at the interruption
what_it_assumes.worry_when: A busy policy period; a national event at the same date; a change in how the outcome was measured or coded at the same date.

what_it_assumes.explains: The line you fit before the interruption is the line the outcome would have continued to follow.
what_it_assumes.title: Functional form of the counterfactual trend
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Few pre-period points; residual autocorrelation that survives the model; the estimate flips when you add a seasonal term or a quadratic trend.

what_it_assumes.explains: No unmeasured confounding of the treatment-outcome relationship, and none of the mediator-outcome relationship either, even after conditioning on treatment.
what_it_assumes.title: Sequential ignorability
what_it_assumes.worry_when: There is a variable affected by treatment that also confounds the mediator-outcome relationship. Under that structure the natural effects are not identified at all.

what_it_assumes.explains: At every period, the things that drive the treatment decision and also affect the outcome are measured -- and measured before that decision.
what_it_assumes.title: No unmeasured time-varying confounding
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Clinical measurements taken after the dose was changed; employment status recorded at the end of a period used to explain treatment at its start.

when_not_to_use: The control has to share the confounding structure. A control chosen for convenience tests nothing, and a null one never rules bias out.
when_to_use: It detects confounding you did not measure, which no balance table can do. In epidemiology it is the standard bias check.

what_it_assumes.worry_when: There was a public announcement well before the policy started, or the pre-period coefficients move in the period immediately before adoption.

what_it_assumes.explains: People could not precisely control which side of the cutoff they landed on.
what_it_assumes.title: No manipulation of the running variable
what_it_assumes.worry_when: A visible spike or gap in the density at the cutoff; covariates that jump; a cutoff that people knew about and had time to respond to.

what_it_assumes.explains: Everything else that affects the outcome changes smoothly through the cutoff, so the only thing that jumps is the treatment.
what_it_assumes.title: Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Several rules share the threshold; the running variable is coarse, so "at the cutoff" is really a wide band; the estimate depends heavily on the bandwidth.

what_it_assumes.explains: The instrument actually moves treatment, and moves it enough that the resulting estimate is not mostly noise.
what_it_assumes.title: Instrument relevance
what_it_assumes.worry_when: An effective F below about 10; a first-stage coefficient that is substantively tiny even if statistically significant; many instruments.

what_it_assumes.explains: The instrument affects the outcome only through the treatment. On the board, that is the arrow you did not draw.
what_it_assumes.title: Exclusion restriction
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The instrument is a policy that changed several things at once; it is correlated with geography, time or institutions that have their own effects; it was chosen because it predicted the outcome.

what_it_assumes.explains: The instrument pushes everyone the same way, or not at all. Nobody takes the treatment only because they were discouraged from it.
what_it_assumes.title: Monotonicity / no defiers
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The instrument is an incentive that could plausibly backfire for some people, or it is a judge or examiner whose leniency ordering differs across case types.

what_it_assumes.explains: The weighted combination of untreated units reproduces the treated unit's pre-period path closely enough to stand in for it afterwards.
what_it_assumes.title: Pre-treatment fit from the donor pool
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Visible pre-period gaps; a short pre-period relative to the number of donors; one donor carrying most of the weight.

what_it_assumes.explains: The treated unit's characteristics can be written as a weighted average of the donors', with weights that do not go negative.
what_it_assumes.title: Treated unit inside the donor convex hull
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The treated unit is at an extreme of the donor distribution on the predictors, or the pre-period gap has a persistent level offset.

what_it_assumes.explains: Nothing else changed at the same moment that also moves the outcome.
what_it_assumes.title: No co-interventions at the interruption
what_it_assumes.worry_when: A busy policy period; a national event at the same date; a change in how the outcome was measured or coded at the same date.

what_it_assumes.explains: The line you fit before the interruption is the line the outcome would have continued to follow.
what_it_assumes.title: Functional form of the counterfactual trend
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Few pre-period points; residual autocorrelation that survives the model; the estimate flips when you add a seasonal term or a quadratic trend.

what_it_assumes.explains: No unmeasured confounding of the treatment-outcome relationship, and none of the mediator-outcome relationship either, even after conditioning on treatment.
what_it_assumes.title: Sequential ignorability
what_it_assumes.worry_when: There is a variable affected by treatment that also confounds the mediator-outcome relationship. Under that structure the natural effects are not identified at all.

what_it_assumes.explains: At every period, the things that drive the treatment decision and also affect the outcome are measured -- and measured before that decision.
what_it_assumes.title: No unmeasured time-varying confounding
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Clinical measurements taken after the dose was changed; employment status recorded at the end of a period used to explain treatment at its start.

when_not_to_use: Shifting the date needs real pre-periods; with two periods there is nowhere to move it to. Permutation asks whether the labelling matters, not whether the design is confounded.
A two-period panel, where there is no pre-period to move the date into
when_to_use: A fake policy date is the single most informative check a difference-in-differences can run, and reshuffling treatment is the cross-sectional version of it.

what_it_assumes.explains: Treated and untreated units are comparable once you condition on the confounders you measured. Everything that pushed people towards treatment and also moves the outcome is in your adjustment set.
what_it_assumes.title: Exchangeability / no unmeasured confounding
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Treatment was chosen by people who knew something about the likely outcome that you do not observe. Clinical judgement, self-selection into a programme, and administrative triage are the classic cases.

what_it_assumes.explains: Every kind of unit had some chance of being treated and some chance of not being treated. Where that fails, there is no comparison to make and the model is inventing one.
what_it_assumes.title: Positivity / overlap
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Any single weight carries a large share of the total; the effective sample is far below the nominal one; the propensity model separates the arms almost perfectly; treated units sit outside the control group's range.

what_it_assumes.explains: One unit's treatment does not change another unit's outcome, and "treated" means the same thing for everyone who got it.
what_it_assumes.title: SUTVA / no interference
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Units interact: they compete for the same jobs, infect each other, share a classroom or a market. Or the "programme" is really a family of programmes whose intensity varied a lot across sites.

what_it_assumes.explains: The outcome you observe under the treatment a unit received is the same as the potential outcome under that treatment. In practice: the treatment has to be a thing someone could actually do.
what_it_assumes.title: Consistency / well-defined intervention
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The treatment is a state of the world rather than an action, or it is coded from several very different real interventions.

when_not_to_use: Every threshold changes the population, so the curve is not repeated attempts at one number. A flat curve says the tails are not driving the result; it says nothing about unmeasured confounding.
when_to_use: Trimming is normally a silent default. This makes it a visible choice, shows what it costs in sample, and marks the variance-minimising threshold rather than inventing a universal one.

methods.title: Triple differences
methods.what_can_go_wrong: It buys robustness with a new assumption: the gap between the two groups inside a unit must have been on parallel paths. If the policy also affected the supposedly unaffected group -- spillovers, general equilibrium -- the third difference subtracts part of the effect. Under staggered adoption the same weighting critique as two-way fixed effects applies, and there is no Callaway-Sant'Anna style version here.
methods.why_recommended: When something else was happening in the treated units at the same time, the third difference sweeps it out: any shock that hit both groups inside a unit and period equally cancels. It rescues designs where plain parallel trends is not credible.

methods.disrecommend_when: Units adopt at more than one date (staggered adoption) and effects may grow over time or differ across cohorts -- then this number is a weighted average of comparisons, not an ATT.

methods.title: ARIMA with an intervention
methods.what_can_go_wrong: The order is chosen by AIC, and near-ties are common; different orders can move the intervention coefficient. Nothing here tests causality: the coefficient is just the size of shift the model wants at that date. Standard errors are asymptotic and optimistic in short series. Simplifications, stated plainly: the search is a small two-stage AIC grid rather than full stepwise auto.arima, no seasonal unit-root test is run, and this is not CausalImpact - there is no Bayesian structural time series and no posterior.
methods.why_recommended: When the series has real memory - last month's value predicts this month's beyond any trend - segmented regression leaves that correlation in the residuals and only patches the standard errors. An ARIMA models it, and its pre-period forecast is an honest, widening counterfactual band.

methods.title: Controlled ITS
methods.what_can_go_wrong: It trades one assumption for another: instead of assuming the trend would have continued, you assume the two series would have moved in parallel. A control that was itself partly exposed pulls the estimate towards zero. Averaging controls that sit at very different levels lets the biggest one decide the answer. Simplification: the interacted model uses Driscoll-Kraay standard errors, which lean on having a reasonable number of periods and are thin on the cross-sectional side when there are only two or three series.
methods.why_recommended: A single interrupted series cannot tell your intervention apart from anything else that happened that month. A control series that was not exposed can, and the control's own level and slope change are reported so you can see whether the shock was shared.

methods.title: Segmented regression
methods.what_can_go_wrong: The counterfactual is a straight line projected forward, and nothing in the data tests it. Anything else that happened at the same date is inside the estimate. Autocorrelated residuals make plain intervals far too narrow, so HAC is the default and the Ljung-Box test is not optional. A regular seasonal cycle that peaks near the interruption will be read as an effect unless you model it. With fewer than about eight pre-period points there is no trend to project. Simplification: the HAC lag is the conventional rule, not a data-driven optimal bandwidth.
methods.why_recommended: It is the standard public-health ITS, it is transparent enough that a reader can check it by eye against the plotted series, and it separates an immediate jump from a change of direction instead of blurring the two into one number.

methods.disrecommend_when: The Olea-Pflueger effective first-stage F is below about 10; report the Anderson-Rubin set instead.

methods.what_can_go_wrong: Exclusion is untestable and usually the weakest link: if the instrument reaches the outcome by any other route, the bias is the violation divided by the first stage, which is enormous when the instrument is weak. methods.title: LIML (and Fuller)
methods.what_can_go_wrong: Exclusion is untestable and usually the weakest link: if the instrument reaches the outcome by any other route, the bias is the violation divided by the first stage, which is enormous when the instrument is weak. Plain LIML has no finite moments, so it occasionally throws out a wild estimate; its interval is wider than the two-stage one and that width is the honest part.
methods.why_recommended: With many instruments or a weak first stage, LIML is approximately median unbiased where two-stage least squares is pulled towards ordinary least squares. Fuller(1) is the better default of the two: it keeps that behaviour and, unlike plain LIML, has finite moments.

methods.title: Randomisation (Fisher) inference
methods.what_can_go_wrong: It tests the sharp null that treatment changed nothing for anyone, which is not the null that the average effect is zero; rejecting it is a weaker statement than it looks. methods.title: Regression kink (the rule bends, it does not switch)
methods.what_can_go_wrong: Estimating a derivative is far noisier than estimating a level, so kink designs need much more data than they look like they need, and they are more sensitive to curvature in the underlying relationship. The number is a change in slope -- per unit of the running variable -- and must never be reported as an effect size. This is capy.py's own local-polynomial code, not rdrobust. The bandwidth selector is named in the Classic tab and the variance is heteroskedasticity- or cluster-robust rather than rdrobust's nearest-neighbour estimator, so numbers will be close but need not match to the last digit.
methods.why_recommended: Benefit formulas, tax schedules and subsidy rules usually bend rather than switch. When that is the rule you have, the kink is the discontinuity, and reading it as a level jump would be wrong.

methods.title: Sharp RD at the cutoff
methods.what_can_go_wrong: The answer is only about units at the cutoff, and it moves with the bandwidth and the polynomial order. If people could see the threshold and push themselves across it, the comparison is gone -- which is why the density test and the covariate jumps travel with the estimate. This is capy.py's own local-polynomial code, not rdrobust. The bandwidth selector is named in the Classic tab and the variance is heteroskedasticity- or cluster-robust rather than rdrobust's nearest-neighbour estimator, so numbers will be close but need not match to the last digit.
methods.why_recommended: When a cutoff really did decide eligibility, the units either side of it are as good as randomly assigned, and you can see the whole argument in one plot. Nothing else in observational work is this legible.

methods.title: Synthetic control
methods.what_can_go_wrong: If the donors cannot reproduce the treated unit before the intervention, the gap afterwards is fit error wearing a policy costume. Weights that pile onto one donor make this a two-unit comparison. With few donors the permutation test cannot produce a small p-value however large the effect, and a donor that had its own shock around the intervention contaminates the comparison. This implementation solves the weight problem with projected gradient plus SLSQP rather than Synth's own solvers, and its cross-validated V is a bounded search, not a global optimum.
methods.why_recommended: For one treated unit and a run of pre-treatment periods this is the standard, and its output is legible to non-specialists: a line, a shadow line, and the distance between them. The weights are transparent, so a reader can argue with the comparison rather than with a coefficient.

methods.title: Augmented synthetic control
methods.what_can_go_wrong: The correction can be larger than the original estimate, at which point the outcome model rather than the donor pool is doing the work. The augmented weights can be negative, which means extrapolating outside the donor pool. This implementation offers ridge ASCM only (no covariate or general outcome-model augmentation), picks the penalty by holding out late pre-treatment periods with the SC weights held fixed, and reports placebo inference rather than augsynth's jackknife+ intervals.
methods.why_recommended: Poor pre-treatment fit is the usual reason a synthetic control fails, and augmentation is the honest response: it estimates the leftover bias and subtracts it, while reporting the uncorrected number beside it so you can see how much of the answer is the correction.

methods.disrecommend_when: Very short panels: with a handful of periods there is no low-rank structure to learn and the fit is mostly the fixed effects.

methods.title: Matrix completion
methods.what_can_go_wrong: There are no donor weights to inspect, so the comparison is much harder to argue with than a synthetic control's. The pre-treatment fit is in-sample and therefore flattering by construction - the placebo-in-time panel is the real check. This implementation uses soft-impute with additive unit and time effects and a single 20% hold-out for the penalty, and its placebo refits reuse that penalty, so the permutation test conditions on it.
methods.why_recommended: It does not need the treated unit to sit inside the donors' convex hull, it uses information from every cell of the panel rather than the treated unit's own history alone, and it handles interactive fixed effects that break parallel trends.

methods.title: Synthetic difference-in-differences
methods.what_can_go_wrong: With one treated unit the paper's jackknife variance is undefined, so inference here is the placebo estimator and rests on donors being exchangeable with the treated unit. Time weights that concentrate on one or two pre-periods make the comparison rest on that slice of history. Covariates are not used at all in this implementation.
methods.why_recommended: It keeps difference-in-differences' tolerance for a permanent level difference between the treated unit and its comparison while borrowing synthetic control's discipline about which units and which periods count. It is usually less sensitive to a poor level match than classic SC and less sensitive to parallel-trends violations than plain DiD.
